title: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB): The Gold Standard for GCA Diagnosis
summary: A definitive surgical diagnostic procedure for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), involving the excision of a 2-3 cm segment of the superficial temporal artery. It remains the gold standard despite advances in non-invasive imaging, crucial for preventing irreversible vision loss from AAION.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) is a specialized surgical procedure to obtain a specimen of the superficial temporal artery (STA) for histopathological analysis. It is primarily indicated when Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)—a systemic granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large-sized vessels—is suspected. Accurate diagnosis is vital to justify long-term, high-dose corticosteroid therapy and its associated morbidity.

branches: Contralateral biopsy if first side is negative (increases yield by 5-10%)
False negative risk (up to 9% due to skips)

rows: New onset or new type of localized pain in the head
Tenderness to palpation or decreased pulsation (not related to arteriosclerosis)
Artery showing vasculitis with mononuclear cell infiltration or granulomatous inflammation

sections.title: Surgical Anatomy: Temple Layers
content: 1. Skin and Subcutaneous Fat
2. Superficial Temporal Fascia (Temporoparietal Fascia - TPF)
3. Subaponeurotic Loose Areolar Tissue
4. Deep Temporal Fascia (Investing Temporalis Muscle)
Note: STA runs WITHIN the TPF/Superficial Fascia.

sections.title: Emergency 'Red Flags' for AAION
content: Sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss
Amaurosis fugax (Transient vision loss)
Chalky white disc edema on fundoscopy
Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Cotton wool spots in a non-diabetic patient

sections.title: Pre-Operative Preparation
content: Palpate STA branches (Frontal vs. Parietal)
Use Doppler Ultrasound to mark the course of the vessel
Consent for facial nerve palsy, scarring, and bleeding
Ensure patient is NOT on anticoagulants if possible (though often continued)
Local anesthesia: Lidocaine 2% with Epinephrine (avoid direct intravascular injection)

sections.title: Step-by-Step Surgical Technique
content: 1. Incision: 3-5cm skin incision over marked vessel course.
2. Blunt Dissection: Through subcutaneous fat to the Superficial Temporal Fascia.
3. Isolation: Identify the pulsating artery; clear fascia using Stevens scissors.
4. Ligation: Proximal and distal ligation using 4-0 Silk or Prolene sutures.
5. Excision: Minimum 2-3 cm segment (account for 10-20% shrinkage).
6. Hemostasis: Meticulous cautery (bipolar preferred).
7. Closure: Two-layer closure (subcutaneous 4-0 Vicryl, skin 5-0 Prolene/Staples).

rows: Proximal muscle pain/stiffness, no vision loss
ANA positive, malar rash, multi-organ involvement
Weight loss, night sweats, localized findings

sections.title: Histopathological Hallmarks
content: Transmural inflammation (Mononuclear cells, macrophages)
Fragmentation of the Internal Elastic Lamina (IEL)
Multinucleated Giant Cells (present in ~50% of positive cases)
Intimal hyperplasia leading to luminal narrowing
Medial thinning and fibrosis

content.explanation: G: Granulomatous inflammation/Great ESR, I: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy, A: Age >50/Artery tenderness, N: Night sweats/New headache, T: Temporal artery biopsy (Gold Standard).

branches: Skin Necrosis (rare, collateral supply usually sufficient)

sections.title: Medical Management Algorithm
content: 1. Suspicion: Start Prednisone 1mg/kg (max 60-80mg) IMMEDIATELY.
2. Biopsy: Perform within 1-2 weeks (results valid even after steroids start).
3. Positive TAB: Taper steroids slowly over 12-24 months based on symptoms/ESR.
4. Steroid Sparing: Consider Tocilizumab (GiACTA trial) or Methotrexate.
5. Relapse: Increase to last effective dose.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A negative biopsy does NOT 100% rule out GCA; treat the patient, not the pathology if clinical suspicion is high.
Jaw claudication is the most specific symptom for GCA (Likelihood Ratio ~9.0).
Perform TAB as soon as possible, but do NOT delay steroids while waiting for the OR.
Always measure the specimen length BEFORE fixation in formalin to ensure adequacy.
The temporal branch of the facial nerve is most vulnerable as it crosses the zygomatic arch (stay superior/anterior).

sections.title: Recent Advances: The TABUL Study
sections.content: The TABUL study compared TAB with Ultrasound (US) for GCA diagnosis. Ultrasound showing the 'Halo Sign' (vessel wall edema) has high specificity but lower sensitivity than TAB. While US is increasingly used as a first-line screen in specialized 'Fast-track' clinics, TAB remains the definitive test for confirmation and for cases where US is indeterminate or negative despite high clinical suspicion.
